analysis.headline: The Shrinkflation Prevention Act never got a hearing or a vote in the House Energy and Commerce Committee before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed the Federal Trade Commission to write rules defining "shrinkflation"—when a company shrinks a product but keeps or raises the price—as an unfair or deceptive practice, and to prohibit it. The FTC and state attorneys general could then enforce those rules against manufacturers. The bill never got a committee hearing or a floor vote and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Shoppers, especially households on tight grocery budgets, who currently absorb hidden price increases when package sizes shrink without a matching price cut.

how_it_helps.text: The bill defines shrinkflation as reducing a product's size or amount without lowering the price by a commensurate amount, and directs the FTC to issue regulations prohibiting manufacturers from the practice within 18 months [S2].

The bill cites Bureau of Labor Statistics data that roughly 10 percent of inflation in some consumer product categories is driven by shrinkflation, and notes consumers are less sensitive to package size changes than to price changes [S2].

Violations would be treated as unfair or deceptive acts under the FTC Act, enforceable by the FTC and by state attorneys general, who could seek injunctions, civil penalties, damages, and restitution on behalf of residents [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Food, beverage, and household-goods manufacturers, who would face federal regulation and enforcement exposure if they downsized products without cutting prices. Consumers might also see more visible price increases if companies stopped using smaller packages as a quieter way to raise prices.

drawbacks.text: Banning shrinkflation does not force companies to charge less; it mainly changes the form a price increase takes. A manufacturer that cannot quietly shrink a package may instead raise the sticker price outright, so the bill protects consumers from deception more than from higher prices [S2].

The statutory definition—requiring price cuts to be "commensurate" with size reductions—leaves significant room for regulatory judgment, and businesses would bear compliance and litigation costs as the FTC and state attorneys general test the rule's boundaries [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the upside is straightforward: fewer silent price increases at the grocery store, with enforcement tools that include restitution. The honest cost is that the bill targets the packaging of price increases rather than their size—companies could respond with visible price hikes instead—and manufacturers would face real compliance and litigation costs. It is a well-aimed transparency-and-enforcement measure rather than a price control, which limits both its benefits and its risks.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to a subcommittee, and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez introduced the bill on March 26, 2024, joined by Rep. Chris Deluzio, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1][S2][S4].
Three days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce, and no further action was ever taken [S4].
The bill attracted 18 cosponsors, all of them House Democrats, and died in committee when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Packaged-food and consumer-goods manufacturers are better off, since they will not face FTC shrinkflation rules or state enforcement actions. Shoppers lost the chance at a remedy for hidden size-based price increases.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 supporters in the record (the sponsor, co-introducer, and 18 cosponsors) were Democrats, and no House Republican signed on; the committee that declined to act was controlled by Republicans [S3][S4].

industries.industry: Packaged food and consumer goods manufacturers
industries.note: The bill would make downsizing products without a matching price cut an FTC-enforceable deceptive practice, with state attorneys general empowered to seek penalties and restitution. Its gain—quiet price increases that shoppers don't notice—comes directly out of shoppers' wallets, so its interest ran against the bill.
Retailers would benefit from clearer, more honest manufacturer pricing, but could face customer complaints and label-adjustment friction when product sizes stabilize or revert.
